sets.title: Geometry: Angles and Lines
sets.description: The building blocks of plane geometry. Angle types, angle pairs, bisectors, and the basic postulates that let you add and compare angles.

cards.front: What is an acute angle?
cards.back: An angle whose measure is greater than 0° and less than 90°.

cards.front: What is a right angle?
cards.back: An angle measuring exactly 90°. Two lines that meet at a right angle are perpendicular.

cards.front: What is an obtuse angle?
cards.back: An angle whose measure is greater than 90° and less than 180°.

cards.front: What is a straight angle?
cards.back: An angle measuring exactly 180°, formed when its two sides point in opposite directions along one line.

cards.front: What are complementary angles?
cards.back: Two angles whose measures add to 90°.

cards.front: What are supplementary angles?
cards.back: Two angles whose measures add to 180°.

cards.front: What are adjacent angles?
cards.back: Two angles that share a vertex and a common side but share no interior points, so they sit side by side without overlapping.

cards.front: What is a linear pair?
cards.back: Two adjacent angles whose non-shared sides form a straight line.

cards.front: What is true of the two angles in a linear pair?
cards.back: They are supplementary, so their measures add to 180°.

cards.front: State the Vertical Angles Theorem.
cards.back: When two lines intersect, the two angles opposite each other at the intersection are congruent.

cards.front: What is an angle bisector?
cards.back: A ray starting at the vertex of an angle that splits it into two congruent angles.

cards.front: State the Angle Bisector Theorem in distance form.
cards.back: A point lies on the bisector of an angle if and only if it is the same distance from both sides of that angle.

cards.front: What is a segment bisector?
cards.back: A line, ray, or segment that passes through the midpoint of a segment, cutting it into two congruent pieces.

cards.front: What is a perpendicular bisector of a segment?
cards.back: A line that passes through the midpoint of the segment and meets it at 90°.

cards.front: State the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem.
cards.back: A point lies on the perpendicular bisector of a segment if and only if it is the same distance from both endpoints of that segment.

cards.front: State the Angle Addition Postulate.
cards.back: If point D lies in the interior of angle ABC, then the measure of angle ABD plus the measure of angle DBC equals the measure of angle ABC.

cards.front: What are skew lines?
cards.back: Two lines that never meet and are not parallel, because they lie in different planes. Skew lines exist only in three dimensions.

sets.title: Geometry: Parallel Lines and Transversals
sets.description: The eight angles made when a transversal crosses two lines. Each angle pair theorem is here along with its converse, which is what you use to prove lines parallel.

cards.front: What is a transversal?
cards.back: A line that crosses two or more other lines at distinct points.

cards.front: What are corresponding angles formed by a transversal?
cards.back: A pair of angles in matching positions at the two intersections, on the same side of the transversal, one interior and one exterior.

cards.front: State the Corresponding Angles Postulate.
cards.back: If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then each pair of corresponding angles is congruent.

cards.front: What are alternate interior angles?
cards.back: A pair of angles that lie between the two lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.

cards.front: State the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem.
cards.back: If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then each pair of alternate interior angles is congruent.

cards.front: What are alternate exterior angles?
cards.back: A pair of angles that lie outside the two lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.

cards.front: State the Alternate Exterior Angles Theorem.
cards.back: If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then each pair of alternate exterior angles is congruent.

cards.front: What are co-interior, or same-side interior, angles?
cards.back: A pair of angles that lie between the two lines and on the same side of the transversal.

cards.front: State the Co-Interior Angles Theorem.
cards.back: If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then each pair of co-interior angles is supplementary, adding to 180°.

cards.front: State the converse of the Corresponding Angles Postulate.
cards.back: If two lines cut by a transversal form a pair of congruent corresponding angles, then the two lines are parallel.

cards.front: State the converse of the Alternate Interior Angles Theorem.
cards.back: If two lines cut by a transversal form a pair of congruent alternate interior angles, then the two lines are parallel.

cards.front: State the converse of the Alternate Exterior Angles Theorem.
cards.back: If two lines cut by a transversal form a pair of congruent alternate exterior angles, then the two lines are parallel.

cards.front: State the converse of the Co-Interior Angles Theorem.
cards.back: If two lines cut by a transversal form a pair of supplementary co-interior angles, then the two lines are parallel.

cards.front: In a plane, what follows if two lines are perpendicular to the same line?
cards.back: The two lines are parallel to each other.

cards.front: If a line is perpendicular to one of two parallel lines, what follows?
cards.back: That line is perpendicular to the other parallel line as well.

cards.front: State the Parallel Postulate.
cards.back: Through a point not on a given line there is exactly one line parallel to the given line.

sets.title: Geometry: Triangle Basics
sets.description: How triangles are classified by sides and by angles, plus the angle sum, exterior angle, inequality, isosceles, and midsegment theorems.

cards.front: State the Triangle Angle Sum Theorem.
cards.back: The three interior angles of any triangle add to 180°.

cards.front: State the Exterior Angle Theorem for a triangle.
cards.back: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, the interior angles not adjacent to it.

cards.front: State the Triangle Inequality Theorem.
cards.back: In any triangle, the sum of the lengths of any two sides is greater than the length of the third side.

cards.front: Given two sides a and b of a triangle, what range holds for the third side c?
cards.back: c must be greater than the positive difference of a and b, and less than the sum a + b.

cards.front: What is a scalene triangle?
cards.back: A triangle with no two sides congruent. Its three angles all have different measures as well.

cards.front: What is an isosceles triangle?
cards.back: A triangle with at least two congruent sides. The congruent sides are the legs and the remaining side is the base.

cards.front: What is an equilateral triangle?
cards.back: A triangle whose three sides are all congruent.

cards.front: Why is every equilateral triangle also equiangular?
cards.back: Congruent sides force congruent opposite angles, so all three angles are equal, and since they total 180° each one measures 60°.

cards.front: State the Isosceles Triangle Theorem.
cards.back: If two sides of a triangle are congruent, then the angles opposite those sides are congruent.

cards.front: State the converse of the Isosceles Triangle Theorem.
cards.back: If two angles of a triangle are congruent, then the sides opposite those angles are congruent, so the triangle is isosceles.

cards.front: What is an acute triangle?
cards.back: A triangle whose three interior angles each measure less than 90°.

cards.front: What is a right triangle?
cards.back: A triangle with exactly one 90° angle. The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse and the other two sides are the legs.

cards.front: What is an obtuse triangle?
cards.back: A triangle with exactly one angle greater than 90°. It cannot have two, because the three angles total only 180°.

cards.front: State the Triangle Midsegment Theorem.
cards.back: The segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half its length.

cards.front: In a triangle, how do the side lengths relate to the opposite angles?
cards.back: The longest side lies opposite the largest angle, and the shortest side lies opposite the smallest angle.

cards.front: What is a median of a triangle?
cards.back: A segment drawn from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. Every triangle has three of them.

cards.front: What is an altitude of a triangle?
cards.back: A segment from a vertex perpendicular to the line containing the opposite side. It serves as the height for that base.

sets.title: Geometry: Triangle Congruence and Similarity
sets.description: The five congruence shortcuts, the two combinations that do not work, and the three similarity criteria. Ends with how length, area, and volume scale.

cards.front: What does CPCTC stand for and mean?
cards.back: Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Congruent. Once two triangles are proved congruent, every matching pair of sides and angles is congruent.

cards.front: What is an included angle?
cards.back: The angle formed between two named sides of a triangle, with its vertex at the point where those two sides meet.

cards.front: What is an included side?
cards.back: The side that lies between two named angles of a triangle, joining their two vertices.

cards.front: State the SSS congruence criterion.
cards.back: If the three sides of one triangle are congruent to the three corresponding sides of another triangle, the two triangles are congruent.

cards.front: State the SAS congruence criterion.
cards.back: If two sides and the included angle of one triangle are congruent to the corresponding two sides and included angle of another, the triangles are congruent.

cards.front: State the ASA congruence criterion.
cards.back: If two angles and the included side of one triangle are congruent to the corresponding two angles and included side of another, the triangles are congruent.

cards.front: State the AAS congruence criterion.
cards.back: If two angles and a non-included side of one triangle are congruent to the corresponding parts of another triangle, the triangles are congruent.

cards.front: State the HL congruence criterion.
cards.back: In two right triangles, if the hypotenuse and one leg of one are congruent to the hypotenuse and corresponding leg of the other, the triangles are congruent.

cards.front: Why is SSA not a valid congruence criterion?
cards.back: Two sides and a non-included angle can often be assembled two different ways, one with an acute angle and one with an obtuse angle. This is the ambiguous case.

cards.front: Why is AAA not a congruence criterion?
cards.back: Matching angles fix the shape but not the size, so AAA triangles can be any scale. AAA proves similarity only.

cards.front: When are two polygons similar?
cards.back: When every pair of corresponding angles is congruent and every pair of corresponding sides is in the same ratio.

cards.front: State the AA similarity criterion.
cards.back: If two angles of one triangle are congruent to two angles of another triangle, the two triangles are similar.

cards.front: State the SSS similarity criterion.
cards.back: If the three pairs of corresponding sides of two triangles are in the same ratio, the two triangles are similar.

cards.front: State the SAS similarity criterion.
cards.back: If two pairs of corresponding sides are in the same ratio and the angles included between those sides are congruent, the triangles are similar.

cards.front: What is the scale factor k between two similar figures?
cards.back: The common ratio of each length in the image to the matching length in the original. It applies to sides, heights, medians, and radii alike.

cards.front: For two similar figures with scale factor k, how do the perimeters compare?
cards.back: The perimeters are in the ratio k, the same ratio as any pair of corresponding lengths.

cards.front: For two similar figures with scale factor k, how do the areas compare?
cards.back: The areas are in the ratio k², so tripling every length multiplies the area by 9.

cards.front: For two similar solids with scale factor k, how do the volumes compare?
cards.back: The volumes are in the ratio k³, so doubling every length multiplies the volume by 8.

cards.front: State the Side-Splitter Theorem.
cards.back: If a line parallel to one side of a triangle crosses the other two sides, it divides those two sides proportionally.

cards.front: State the Triangle Angle Bisector Theorem.
cards.back: The bisector of an angle of a triangle divides the opposite side into two segments proportional to the two sides that form that angle.

sets.title: Geometry: Right Triangles
sets.description: The Pythagorean Theorem and its converse, the common triples, the two special right triangles, and the geometric mean relationships made by the altitude to the hypotenuse.

cards.front: State the Pythagorean Theorem.
cards.back: In a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c, a² + b² = c².

cards.front: State the converse of the Pythagorean Theorem.
cards.back: If a triangle has sides a, b, and c with c the longest and a² + b² = c², then the triangle is a right triangle with its right angle opposite side c.

cards.front: How do you test whether a triangle is acute from its three sides?
cards.back: With c as the longest side, the triangle is acute when a² + b² is greater than c².

cards.front: How do you test whether a triangle is obtuse from its three sides?
cards.back: With c as the longest side, the triangle is obtuse when a² + b² is less than c².

cards.front: What is a Pythagorean triple?
cards.back: A set of three positive whole numbers a, b, and c satisfying a² + b² = c², so they can be the side lengths of a right triangle.

cards.front: Name the smallest Pythagorean triple.
cards.back: 3, 4, 5, since 9 + 16 = 25. Any multiple such as 6, 8, 10 or 9, 12, 15 is also a triple.

cards.front: Name the Pythagorean triple whose hypotenuse is 13.
Name the Pythagorean triple whose smallest side is 8.
Name the Pythagorean triple whose smallest side is 7.
What are the side ratios in a 45-45-90 triangle?
cards.back: The two legs are equal and the hypotenuse is a leg × sqrt(2), so the sides are in the ratio 1 : 1 : sqrt(2).

cards.front: In a 45-45-90 triangle, how do you find a leg from the hypotenuse?
cards.back: Divide the hypotenuse by sqrt(2), which is the same as multiplying it by sqrt(2)/2.

cards.front: What are the side ratios in a 30-60-90 triangle?
cards.back: The sides are in the ratio 1 : sqrt(3) : 2, with 1 opposite the 30° angle, sqrt(3) opposite the 60° angle, and 2 as the hypotenuse.

cards.front: In a 30-60-90 triangle, how is the short leg related to the hypotenuse?
cards.back: The short leg, the one opposite the 30° angle, is exactly half the hypotenuse.

cards.front: What is the geometric mean of two positive numbers a and b?
cards.back: sqrt(a × b), the positive number x for which a/x = x/b.

cards.front: Why does the altitude to the hypotenuse create similar triangles?
cards.back: In a right triangle it forms two smaller right triangles that each share an acute angle with the original, so all three triangles are similar by AA.

cards.front: State the geometric mean altitude theorem.
cards.back: In a right triangle, the altitude to the hypotenuse is the geometric mean of the two hypotenuse pieces it creates, so h = sqrt(p × q).

cards.front: State the geometric mean leg theorem.
cards.back: In a right triangle, each leg is the geometric mean of the whole hypotenuse and the hypotenuse piece adjacent to that leg.

cards.front: How does the Pythagorean Theorem give the distance between two points?
cards.back: The horizontal and vertical gaps are the legs of a right triangle and the distance is the hypotenuse, so distance = sqrt((change in x)² + (change in y)²).

sets.title: Geometry: Triangle Centers
sets.description: The four classic centers of a triangle. What each one is the intersection of, what it is equidistant from, and when it lands outside the triangle.

cards.front: What is the centroid of a triangle?
cards.back: The point where the three medians meet. It is the balance point, or center of mass, of the triangle.

cards.front: State the centroid 2:1 property.
cards.back: The centroid divides each median so the piece from the vertex is twice as long as the piece from the centroid to the midpoint of the opposite side.

cards.front: Can the centroid ever fall outside the triangle?
cards.back: No. The centroid always lies inside, because every median runs from a vertex into the interior.

cards.front: What is the incenter of a triangle?
cards.back: The point where the three angle bisectors meet.

cards.front: What is the incenter equidistant from?
cards.back: The three sides of the triangle. That shared distance is the radius of the inscribed circle.

cards.front: Can the incenter ever fall outside the triangle?
cards.back: No. The incenter always lies inside, because the inscribed circle has to touch all three sides.

cards.front: What is the circumcenter of a triangle?
cards.back: The point where the three perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet.

cards.front: What is the circumcenter equidistant from?
cards.back: The three vertices of the triangle. That shared distance is the radius of the circumscribed circle.

cards.front: Where does the circumcenter sit for acute, right, and obtuse triangles?
cards.back: Inside an acute triangle, exactly at the midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right triangle, and outside an obtuse triangle.

cards.front: What is the orthocenter of a triangle?
cards.back: The point where the three altitudes, or the lines containing them, meet.

cards.front: Where does the orthocenter sit for acute, right, and obtuse triangles?
cards.back: Inside an acute triangle, at the right-angle vertex of a right triangle, and outside an obtuse triangle.

cards.front: Which triangle centers can fall outside the triangle?
cards.back: Only the circumcenter and the orthocenter, and each lands outside exactly when the triangle is obtuse.

cards.front: What is the incircle of a triangle?
cards.back: The circle centered at the incenter that is tangent to all three sides from the inside.

cards.front: What is the circumcircle of a triangle?
cards.back: The circle centered at the circumcenter that passes through all three vertices.

cards.front: What is the Euler line of a triangle?
cards.back: The single line that contains the centroid, the circumcenter, and the orthocenter of any triangle that is not equilateral.

cards.front: Where does the centroid sit along the Euler line?
cards.back: Between the orthocenter and the circumcenter, twice as far from the orthocenter as it is from the circumcenter.

cards.front: What is special about the centers of an equilateral triangle?
cards.back: The centroid, incenter, circumcenter, and orthocenter all land on the same point.

sets.title: Geometry: Quadrilaterals
sets.description: Parallelograms, rectangles, rhombuses, squares, trapezoids, and kites. Each property is separated from the tests used to prove a figure belongs to the family.

cards.front: What is a parallelogram?
cards.back: A quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel.

cards.front: In a parallelogram, what is true of the opposite sides?
cards.back: They are congruent as well as parallel.

cards.front: In a parallelogram, what is true of the opposite angles?
cards.back: They are congruent.

cards.front: In a parallelogram, what is true of consecutive angles?
cards.back: They are supplementary, adding to 180°, because they are co-interior angles between a pair of parallel sides.

cards.front: In a parallelogram, what is true of the diagonals?
cards.back: They bisect each other, meeting at a point that is the midpoint of both.

cards.front: Which condition on one pair of sides proves a parallelogram?
cards.back: If one pair of opposite sides of a quadrilateral is both parallel and congruent, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

cards.front: Which condition on the diagonals proves a parallelogram?
cards.back: If the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

cards.front: What is a rectangle?
cards.back: A parallelogram with four right angles.

cards.front: What is true of the diagonals of a rectangle?
cards.back: They are congruent, and because a rectangle is a parallelogram they also bisect each other.

cards.front: What is a rhombus?
cards.back: A parallelogram with four congruent sides.

cards.front: What is true of the diagonals of a rhombus?
cards.back: They are perpendicular to each other, and each diagonal bisects a pair of opposite angles.

cards.front: What is a square?
cards.back: A quadrilateral that is both a rectangle and a rhombus, so it has four right angles and four congruent sides.

cards.front: What is a trapezoid?
cards.back: Using the inclusive definition, a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides, called the bases. The other two sides are the legs.

cards.front: What is an isosceles trapezoid?
cards.back: A trapezoid whose legs, the two non-parallel sides, are congruent.

cards.front: What is true of the base angles of an isosceles trapezoid?
cards.back: The two angles along each base are congruent.

cards.front: What is true of the diagonals of an isosceles trapezoid?
cards.back: They are congruent.

cards.front: State the Trapezoid Midsegment Theorem.
cards.back: The segment joining the midpoints of the legs is parallel to both bases, and its length is (b1 + b2)/2, the average of the two bases.

cards.front: What is a kite?
cards.back: A quadrilateral with two distinct pairs of congruent adjacent sides.

cards.front: What is true of the diagonals of a kite?
cards.back: They are perpendicular, and the diagonal joining the vertices between the pairs of congruent sides bisects the other diagonal.

cards.front: How does the quadrilateral hierarchy fit together?
cards.back: Every square is both a rhombus and a rectangle, every rhombus and rectangle is a parallelogram, and under the inclusive definition every parallelogram is a trapezoid.

sets.title: Geometry: Polygons
sets.description: Angle sums, diagonal counts, and naming for polygons with any number of sides, plus the formulas that apply only to regular polygons.

cards.front: What is a polygon?
cards.back: A closed plane figure built from three or more straight segments that meet only at their endpoints, with no side crossing another.

cards.front: Formula for the sum of the interior angles of a polygon with n sides.
cards.back: Interior angle sum = (n - 2) × 180°.

cards.front: Why does the interior angle sum formula use (n - 2)?
cards.back: Drawing all diagonals from one vertex splits an n-sided polygon into n - 2 triangles, and each triangle contributes 180°.

cards.front: What is the sum of the exterior angles of a convex polygon?
cards.back: 360°, taking one exterior angle at each vertex, no matter how many sides the polygon has.

cards.front: What is a regular polygon?
cards.back: A polygon that is both equilateral, meaning all sides are congruent, and equiangular, meaning all angles are congruent.

cards.front: Formula for one interior angle of a regular polygon with n sides.
cards.back: Each interior angle = (n - 2) × 180° ÷ n.

cards.front: Formula for one exterior angle of a regular polygon with n sides.
cards.back: Each exterior angle = 360° ÷ n.

cards.front: Formula for the number of diagonals of a polygon with n sides.
cards.back: Number of diagonals = n × (n - 3) ÷ 2.

cards.front: How many diagonals can be drawn from a single vertex of an n-gon?
cards.back: n - 3, because a vertex cannot join to itself or to either of its two neighbours.

cards.front: What is a convex polygon?
cards.back: A polygon whose every interior angle is less than 180°, so no vertex points inward and every diagonal stays inside the figure.

cards.front: What is a concave polygon?
cards.back: A polygon with at least one interior angle greater than 180°, which pushes at least one diagonal outside the figure.

cards.front: Name the polygons with 5, 6, 7, and 8 sides.
cards.back: Pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, and octagon.

cards.front: Name the polygons with 9, 10, and 12 sides.
cards.back: Nonagon, decagon, and dodecagon.

cards.front: What is each interior angle of a regular pentagon?
What is each interior angle of a regular hexagon?
What is the apothem of a regular polygon?
cards.back: The perpendicular segment from the center to the midpoint of a side. Every apothem of a given regular polygon has the same length.

sets.title: Geometry: Circles, Parts and Angles
sets.description: Vocabulary for the pieces of a circle, then every rule for measuring an angle from the arcs it intercepts, whether its vertex is on, inside, or outside the circle.

cards.front: What is the radius of a circle?
cards.back: A segment from the center to any point on the circle. Every such segment in one circle has the same length.

cards.front: What is a diameter of a circle?
cards.back: A chord that passes through the center. Its length is twice the radius.

cards.front: What is a chord?
cards.back: A segment whose two endpoints both lie on the circle.

cards.front: What is a secant of a circle?
cards.back: A line that crosses the circle at two points. It contains a chord and extends beyond it in both directions.

cards.front: What is a tangent to a circle?
cards.back: A line that touches the circle at exactly one point, called the point of tangency.

cards.front: What is an arc of a circle?
cards.back: A connected piece of the circle between two points on it.

cards.front: What separates a minor arc from a major arc?
cards.back: A minor arc measures less than 180° and a major arc measures greater than 180°.

cards.front: What is a semicircle?
cards.back: An arc measuring exactly 180°, cut off by a diameter, so it is half the circle.

cards.front: What is a central angle?
cards.back: An angle whose vertex is the center of the circle. Its measure equals the measure of the arc it intercepts.

cards.front: What is an inscribed angle?
cards.back: An angle whose vertex lies on the circle and whose two sides are chords of that circle.

cards.front: State the Inscribed Angle Theorem.
cards.back: An inscribed angle measures half its intercepted arc, so it is half of the central angle that intercepts the same arc.

cards.front: What is true of two inscribed angles that intercept the same arc?
cards.back: They are congruent, because each one measures half of that arc.

cards.front: State Thales' Theorem, the angle in a semicircle.
cards.back: An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle, because its intercepted arc measures 180° and the inscribed angle is half of that.

cards.front: What is true of the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral?
cards.back: For a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle, each pair of opposite angles is supplementary, adding to 180°.

cards.front: How do you measure an angle formed by two chords meeting inside a circle?
cards.back: It measures half the sum of the two intercepted arcs, the arc it opens onto and the arc its vertical angle opens onto.

cards.front: How do you measure an angle formed by two secants meeting outside a circle?
cards.back: It measures half the difference of the two intercepted arcs, the far arc minus the near arc.

cards.front: State the tangent-chord angle rule.
cards.back: An angle formed by a tangent and a chord meeting at the point of tangency measures half the arc that lies inside the angle.

cards.front: How do you measure an angle formed by a tangent and a secant meeting outside a circle?
cards.back: It measures half the difference of the two intercepted arcs, the far arc minus the near arc.

cards.front: What are concentric circles?
cards.back: Two or more circles that share the same center but have different radii.

sets.title: Geometry: Circles, Segments and Measures
sets.description: Circumference, area, arc length, and sector area, plus the tangent and chord relationships, the power of a point rules, and the equation of a circle.

cards.front: Formula for the circumference of a circle.
cards.back: C = 2 × π × r, which is the same as π × d where d is the diameter.

cards.front: Formula for the area of a circle.
cards.back: A = π × r².

cards.front: Formula for the length of an arc with a central angle of n degrees in a circle of radius r.
cards.back: Arc length = (n/360) × 2 × π × r.

cards.front: Formula for the area of a sector with a central angle of n degrees and radius r.
cards.back: Sector area = (n/360) × π × r².

cards.front: How do you find the area of a circular segment?
cards.back: Find the area of the sector for that central angle, then subtract the area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord.

cards.front: What is the difference between arc measure and arc length?
cards.back: Arc measure is the angle in degrees that the arc covers. Arc length is an actual distance and depends on the radius as well as the angle.

cards.front: How does a tangent line relate to the radius at the point of tangency?
cards.back: The tangent line is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of tangency.

cards.front: State the Two Tangent Segments Theorem.
cards.back: Two tangent segments drawn to the same circle from a single external point are congruent.

cards.front: What happens when a radius is perpendicular to a chord?
cards.back: It bisects that chord and also bisects the arc the chord cuts off.

cards.front: How do congruent chords relate to the center of a circle?
cards.back: Two chords of the same circle are congruent if and only if they are the same distance from the center.

cards.front: State the chord-chord power of a point rule.
cards.back: If two chords meet inside a circle, the products of the two pieces of each chord are equal, so a × b = c × d.

cards.front: State the secant-secant power of a point rule.
cards.back: For two secants drawn from one external point, the whole secant times its external part gives the same product for both secants.

cards.front: State the tangent-secant power of a point rule.
cards.back: For a tangent of length t and a secant drawn from the same external point, t² equals the whole secant times its external part.

cards.front: State the equation of a circle with center (h, k) and radius r.
cards.back: (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r².

cards.front: What is the equation of a circle centered at the origin with radius r?
cards.back: x² + y² = r².

cards.front: How do you find the center and radius from a general circle equation?
cards.back: Complete the square in x and again in y to reach the form (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r², then read off the center (h, k) and take the square root for r.

cards.front: What ratio defines the number π?
cards.back: The circumference of any circle divided by its diameter, a value of about 3.14159 for every circle.

cards.front: How many radians are in a full circle?
cards.back: 2 × π radians equal 360°, so one radian is 180 ÷ π degrees, roughly 57.3°.

cards.front: How do you convert a degree measure to radians?
cards.back: Multiply the degree measure by π/180.

sets.title: Geometry: Area and Perimeter
sets.description: One formula per card for the areas of the standard plane figures, plus how to handle composite shapes and how area behaves when lengths change.

cards.front: What is perimeter?
cards.back: The total distance around the outside of a plane figure, found by adding the lengths of all its sides.

cards.front: Formula for the area of a rectangle.
cards.back: Area = length × width.

cards.front: Formula for the perimeter of a rectangle.
cards.back: Perimeter = 2 × length + 2 × width.

cards.front: Formula for the area of a square with side s.
cards.back: Area = s², the side length squared.

cards.front: Formula for the perimeter of a square with side s.
cards.back: Perimeter = 4 × s.

cards.front: Formula for the area of a triangle from base and height.
cards.back: Area = (1/2) × base × height, where the height is measured perpendicular to the chosen base.

cards.front: State Heron's formula for the area of a triangle.
cards.back: With sides a, b, c and semiperimeter s = (a + b + c)/2, area = sqrt(s × (s - a) × (s - b) × (s - c)).

cards.front: Formula for the area of an equilateral triangle with side s.
cards.back: Area = (sqrt(3)/4) × s².

cards.front: Formula for the area of a parallelogram.
cards.back: Area = base × height, where the height is the perpendicular distance between the parallel bases, not the length of the slanted side.

cards.front: Formula for the area of a trapezoid.
cards.back: Area = (1/2) × (b1 + b2) × h, where b1 and b2 are the parallel bases and h is the perpendicular distance between them.

cards.front: Formula for the area of a rhombus from its diagonals.
cards.back: Area = (1/2) × d1 × d2, half the product of the two diagonal lengths.

cards.front: Formula for the area of a kite from its diagonals.
cards.back: Area = (1/2) × d1 × d2, the same rule that works for any quadrilateral whose diagonals are perpendicular.

cards.front: Formula for the area of a rhombus from a side and a height.
cards.back: Area = base × height, because every rhombus is a parallelogram.

cards.front: Formula for the area of a regular polygon using the apothem.
cards.back: Area = (1/2) × apothem × perimeter.

cards.front: How do you find the area of a composite figure?
cards.back: Break it into shapes you have formulas for, add those areas together, and subtract the area of any region that has been cut out.

cards.front: What happens to the area of a figure when every length is doubled?
cards.back: The area is multiplied by 4, because area scales by the square of the factor applied to the lengths.

cards.front: How do the units of area compare with the units of perimeter?
cards.back: Perimeter uses linear units such as cm. Area uses square units such as cm².

sets.title: Geometry: Solids
sets.description: Surface area and volume for prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, spheres, and cubes, plus nets, cross sections, and Euler's formula.

cards.front: What is a prism?
cards.back: A solid with two congruent parallel bases joined by parallelogram faces. It is named for the shape of its base, as in a triangular prism.

cards.front: Formula for the volume of a prism.
cards.back: Volume = B × h, the area of one base times the perpendicular height.

cards.front: Formula for the surface area of a right prism.
cards.back: Surface area = 2 × B + P × h, where B is the base area, P is the base perimeter, and h is the height.

cards.front: What is the difference between lateral and total surface area?
cards.back: Lateral surface area counts only the side faces of a solid. Total surface area adds in the area of the base or bases.

cards.front: Formula for the volume of a cylinder.
cards.back: Volume = π × r² × h.

cards.front: Formula for the surface area of a right cylinder.
cards.back: Surface area = 2 × π × r² + 2 × π × r × h, the two circular bases plus the curved side.

cards.front: Formula for the volume of a pyramid.
cards.back: Volume = (1/3) × B × h, one third of the base area times the perpendicular height.

cards.front: Formula for the surface area of a regular pyramid.
cards.back: Surface area = B + (1/2) × P × l, where B is the base area, P is the base perimeter, and l is the slant height.

cards.front: Formula for the volume of a cone.
cards.back: Volume = (1/3) × π × r² × h.

cards.front: Formula for the surface area of a right cone.
cards.back: Surface area = π × r² + π × r × l, the circular base plus the curved side, where l is the slant height.

cards.front: How is the slant height of a right cone found from r and h?
cards.back: l = sqrt(r² + h²), by applying the Pythagorean Theorem to the radius and the height.

cards.front: Formula for the surface area of a sphere.
cards.back: Surface area = 4 × π × r².

cards.front: Formula for the volume of a sphere.
cards.back: Volume = (4/3) × π × r³.

cards.front: Formula for the volume of a cube with edge s.
cards.back: Volume = s³.

cards.front: Formula for the surface area of a cube with edge s.
cards.back: Surface area = 6 × s², since a cube has six congruent square faces.

cards.front: How do the volumes of a cone and a cylinder with the same base and height compare?
cards.back: The cone holds one third as much as the cylinder. The same one to three ratio holds between a pyramid and a prism.

cards.front: State Euler's formula for polyhedra.
cards.back: For any convex polyhedron, V - E + F = 2, where V counts vertices, E counts edges, and F counts faces.

cards.front: What is a net of a solid?
cards.back: A flat pattern of all the faces that folds up into the solid. The total area of the net equals the surface area of the solid.

cards.front: What is a cross section of a solid?
cards.back: The two-dimensional figure formed where a plane slices through the solid.

cards.front: What cross sections can a cylinder produce?
cards.back: A circle when the cut is parallel to the bases, a rectangle when it is perpendicular and passes through the axis, and an ellipse when the cut is slanted.

sets.title: Geometry: Coordinate Geometry
sets.description: Distance, midpoint, and slope on the coordinate plane, the three forms of a linear equation, and how to prove a figure is what it looks like from its vertices.

cards.front: State the distance formula in the coordinate plane.
cards.back: The distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is sqrt((x2 - x1)² + (y2 - y1)²).

cards.front: State the midpoint formula.
cards.back: The midpoint of the segment from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2) is ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2).

cards.front: Formula for the slope of a line through two points.
cards.back: Slope m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1), the change in y divided by the change in x.

cards.front: What is the slope of a horizontal line?
cards.back: Zero, because the change in y between any two of its points is 0.

cards.front: What is the slope of a vertical line?
cards.back: Undefined, because the change in x is 0 and division by zero has no value.

cards.front: How do the slopes of parallel lines compare?
cards.back: Two non-vertical lines are parallel exactly when their slopes are equal and their y-intercepts differ.

cards.front: How do the slopes of perpendicular lines compare?
cards.back: They are negative reciprocals, so m1 × m2 = -1. The exception is a vertical line paired with a horizontal line.

cards.front: State the slope-intercept form of a line.
cards.back: y = m × x + b, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept.

cards.front: State the point-slope form of a line.
cards.back: y - y1 = m × (x - x1), for the line with slope m passing through the point (x1, y1).

cards.front: State the standard form of a linear equation.
cards.back: A × x + B × y = C, where A, B, and C are constants and A and B are not both zero. When B is not 0 the slope is -A/B.

cards.front: What is the equation of the horizontal line through (a, b)?
cards.back: y = b, since every point on the line shares the same y-coordinate.

cards.front: What is the equation of the vertical line through (a, b)?
cards.back: x = a, since every point on the line shares the same x-coordinate.

cards.front: How do you find the point that partitions a segment in the ratio a to b?
cards.back: From (x1, y1), move a/(a + b) of the way: x = x1 + (a/(a + b)) × (x2 - x1) and y = y1 + (a/(a + b)) × (y2 - y1).

cards.front: How do you check whether three points are collinear?
cards.back: Find the slope between the first pair and the slope between the second pair. Equal slopes mean the three points lie on one line.

cards.front: How do you prove a quadrilateral on the coordinate plane is a parallelogram?
cards.back: Show both pairs of opposite sides have equal slopes, or show the two diagonals share the same midpoint.

cards.front: How do you prove a quadrilateral on the coordinate plane is a rhombus?
cards.back: Show it is a parallelogram, then use the distance formula to show all four sides have the same length.

cards.front: How do you prove a triangle on the coordinate plane is a right triangle?
cards.back: Show two sides have slopes whose product is -1, or find the three side lengths and check them against the Pythagorean Theorem.

cards.front: How do you find the perimeter of a polygon from its vertices?
cards.back: Apply the distance formula to each pair of consecutive vertices, then add all the side lengths together.

cards.front: Given (x - 2)² + (y + 3)² = 25, what are the center and radius?
cards.back: The center is (2, -3) and the radius is 5. Read h and k with their signs reversed, then take the square root of 25.

sets.title: Geometry: Transformations
sets.description: Translations, reflections, rotations, and dilations with their coordinate rules, which ones preserve congruence, and how symmetry is defined.

cards.front: What is a translation?
cards.back: A rigid motion that slides every point of a figure the same distance in the same direction. In coordinates, (x, y) maps to (x + a, y + b).

cards.front: What is a reflection?
cards.back: A rigid motion that flips a figure across a line so each point and its image sit the same distance from that line, on opposite sides.

cards.front: Coordinate rule for a reflection across the x-axis.
cards.back: (x, y) maps to (x, -y).

cards.front: Coordinate rule for a reflection across the y-axis.
cards.back: (x, y) maps to (-x, y).

cards.front: Coordinate rule for a reflection across the line y = x.
cards.back: (x, y) maps to (y, x), so the two coordinates trade places.

cards.front: Coordinate rule for a reflection through the origin.
cards.back: (x, y) maps to (-x, -y). This gives the same image as a 180° rotation about the origin.

cards.front: What is a rotation?
cards.back: A rigid motion that turns every point of a figure about a fixed center through a given angle, keeping each point the same distance from that center.

cards.front: Coordinate rule for a 90° counterclockwise rotation about the origin.
cards.back: (x, y) maps to (-y, x).

cards.front: Coordinate rule for a 180° rotation about the origin.
cards.back: (x, y) maps to (-x, -y). The direction of the turn does not matter for 180°.

cards.front: Coordinate rule for a 270° counterclockwise rotation about the origin.
cards.back: (x, y) maps to (y, -x), which is the same as a 90° clockwise turn.

cards.front: What is a dilation?
cards.back: A transformation that scales a figure toward or away from a fixed center by a factor k, multiplying every distance from that center by k.

cards.front: Coordinate rule for a dilation centered at the origin with scale factor k.
cards.back: (x, y) maps to (k × x, k × y).

cards.front: What does a dilation with a scale factor between 0 and 1 do?
cards.back: It shrinks the figure toward the center. A scale factor greater than 1 enlarges the figure instead.

cards.front: Which transformations preserve congruence?
cards.back: Translations, reflections, and rotations, known together as rigid motions or isometries. Each one keeps every length and every angle unchanged.

cards.front: Which transformation preserves shape but not size?
cards.back: A dilation with a scale factor other than 1. Its image is ~ to the original but not ≅ to it.

cards.front: What is a composition of transformations?
cards.back: Applying one transformation and then applying another to the result. Changing the order usually changes the final image.

cards.front: What is a glide reflection?
cards.back: The composition of a translation along a line with a reflection across that same line. It is a rigid motion.

cards.front: What is line symmetry?
cards.back: A figure has line symmetry when reflecting it across some line maps the figure exactly onto itself. That line is a line of symmetry.

cards.front: What is rotational symmetry?
cards.back: A figure has rotational symmetry when a rotation of less than 360° about its center maps the figure exactly onto itself.

cards.front: How many lines of symmetry does a regular polygon with n sides have?
cards.back: Exactly n. It also has rotational symmetry for every turn of 360° ÷ n.
